title: TypeScript Mastery
subtitle: 26 weeks from `const` to conditional types — every chapter, in order, with problems, a build project and an end-of-week exam.
intro: This is the Learn library turned into a programme. Each week gives you a small number of chapters to study, curated problems from the Library to apply them, a build project of your own, and a quiz you must pass to unlock the next week. Weeks ahead of you stay sealed — the point is to go in order. Weeks behind you stay open forever.

weeks.title: Values, Types & Inference
weeks.goal: Declare and annotate values, and understand what TypeScript works out on its own.

problems.note: Your first program: read a line, print a line.
Parse two numbers and print their sum.
Store intermediate results in well-named constants.
Get comfortable with the stdin/stdout contract.

weeks.project: Write a `units.ts` that reads a temperature in Celsius and prints it in Fahrenheit and Kelvin, using `const` throughout and one explicit annotation per value.

quiz.question: Which declaration should you reach for by default?
options: const, switching to let only when you must reassign
let, because const is for compile-time constants
var, which is the most compatible
quiz.explanation: `const` locks the binding, which removes a whole class of accidental reassignment. Reach for `let` only when the value genuinely changes.

quiz.question: What type does `const x = 5` have?
options: The literal type 5, because const bindings cannot change
It has no type until annotated
quiz.explanation: A `const` binding to a primitive infers the literal type, since it can never hold anything else. `let y = 5` widens to `number`.

quiz.question: Why prefer `unknown` over `any` for a value of uncertain type?
options: unknown forces you to narrow before using it; any turns checking off entirely
any cannot be assigned to variables
There is no difference under strict mode
quiz.explanation: `any` silently disables every check that follows it. `unknown` keeps the value opaque until you prove what it is.

quiz.question: `let count = 0; count = "zero";` — what happens?
options: A compile error: count was inferred as number
It works; TypeScript widens count to any
It works, but only outside strict mode
quiz.explanation: Inference from the initializer is binding. `count` is `number` from that point on, so assigning a string is rejected at compile time.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `let x` and `const x` at block scope?
options: const cannot be rebound; both are scoped to the enclosing { }
const is function-scoped, let is block-scoped
There is none in modern TypeScript
quiz.explanation: `const` blocks reassignment of the NAME. A const object's contents are still mutable — that is `readonly`'s job, not const's.

quiz.question: `const x: any = "hi"; x.notAMethod();` — what does the compiler say?
options: Nothing; any disables checking for that value
Property does not exist on type string
any is not assignable to string
quiz.explanation: That silence is the whole problem with `any`, and the reason `unknown` is the right escape hatch when you genuinely do not know a type.

exam.title: Temperature table
exam.prompt: The input is a line of Celsius temperatures. For each one print `C=F` where F is `C * 9 / 5 + 32`, one per line, then print the count on the last line.
exam.hint: Declare each converted value with const inside the loop; TypeScript infers number throughout.

weeks.title: Operators & Control Flow
weeks.goal: Branch correctly, and know exactly which values are falsy.

problems.note: A rule with nested exceptions — get the && / || precedence right.

weeks.project: Write a `grade.ts` that reads a score and prints a letter grade, then a second version using a lookup table instead of an if-chain. Compare which one you would rather extend.

quiz.question: Why should you always use `===` instead of `==`?
options: `==` coerces its operands, so "1" == 1 is true and the rules are hard to predict
`==` is deprecated and errors under strict
`===` also compares object identity, which `==` cannot
quiz.explanation: Loose equality applies a conversion table almost nobody has memorised. Strict equality compares type and value with no surprises.

quiz.question: Which of these is truthy?
quiz.explanation: Any non-empty string is truthy, including "0" and "false". The falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN.

quiz.question: What does `a ?? b` do that `a || b` does not?
options: It falls back only for null/undefined, so 0 and "" pass through
It throws when a is null
quiz.explanation: `||` falls back on every falsy value, which silently replaces legitimate zeros and empty strings. `??` triggers only on nullish values.

quiz.question: `obj?.prop` where `obj` is undefined evaluates to…
quiz.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits the whole access and produces `undefined` rather than throwing.

quiz.question: `if (value)` where `value` is `0` — does the branch run?
quiz.explanation: 0 is falsy, which is why truthiness checks silently swallow legitimate zeros. Compare explicitly when 0 is a valid value.

quiz.question: What does `switch` compare cases with?
quiz.explanation: `switch` uses strict equality, so `case "1"` never matches the number 1 — the same discipline as writing === everywhere else.

exam.title: Ticket price
exam.prompt: The input is `age isMember` (the second is `yes` or `no`). Base price is 20. Under 13 pays half; 65 and over pays 15; members get 5 off after that, but the price never drops below 0. Print the price, then `member` or `guest`.
exam.hint: Resolve the age band first with if/else if, then apply the member discount to whatever that produced.

weeks.title: Loops & Numbers
weeks.goal: Iterate deliberately, and know where floating-point arithmetic bites.

problems.note: Build output in a loop rather than a string concat chain.
Watch the growth — when does a number stop being exact?
Stop the loop at the square root, not at n.

weeks.project: Write a `stats.ts` that reads a line of numbers and prints their count, sum, mean and range — one pass, no array methods.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `for...of` and `for...in` over an array?
options: for...of yields the values; for...in yields the string keys
They are the same for arrays
for...in yields values, for...of yields indices
for...in does not work on arrays
quiz.explanation: `for...in` enumerates keys as strings — including inherited ones — which is almost never what you want for an array.

quiz.question: Why is `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` false?
options: number is a 64-bit float, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation
It is true under strict mode
quiz.explanation: Binary floating point cannot represent these decimals exactly. Compare with a tolerance, or work in integers (cents rather than dollars).

quiz.question: What does `Math.trunc(-4.7)` return?
quiz.explanation: `trunc` drops the fractional part toward zero. `Math.floor(-4.7)` is -5, which is the usual source of confusion.

quiz.question: What is the largest exactly-representable integer?
options: There is no limit; number is arbitrary precision
quiz.explanation: Past 2^53 - 1 consecutive integers stop being distinguishable. `bigint` exists for values beyond that.

quiz.question: Which loop gives you the index and works with `break`?
options: A classic for loop, or for...of with .entries()
quiz.explanation: `forEach` cannot be broken out of — `return` only skips one callback. Reach for `for...of` when you need early exit.

quiz.question: `Math.round(-2.5)` returns…
quiz.explanation: `Math.round` breaks ties toward positive infinity, so -2.5 rounds to -2. Use Math.floor or trunc when you need a predictable direction.

exam.title: Number report
exam.prompt: The input is one integer `n` (at least 1). Print four lines: the sum 1..n, the count of divisors of n, whether n is prime, and the number of digits in n.
exam.hint: A number is prime exactly when it has two divisors. Use Math.trunc when peeling digits so negatives and floats cannot creep in.

weeks.title: Text & String Methods
weeks.goal: Manipulate strings fluently and remember that they are immutable.

problems.note: Split, reverse, join — or an index loop.
Scan characters with a membership test.
Split on whitespace and mind the empty pieces.

weeks.project: Write a `slug.ts` that turns a title into a URL slug: lowercase, non-alphanumerics to hyphens, collapse runs, trim the ends.

quiz.question: What does `s.replace("a", "b")` do when `s` contains several `a`s?
options: Throws unless a regex is used
quiz.explanation: A string pattern replaces one occurrence. Use `replaceAll`, or a regex with the `g` flag, for every match.

quiz.question: What does `"abcdef".slice(-2)` return?
quiz.explanation: A negative index counts back from the end. `substring` does not support this and clamps negatives to 0.

quiz.question: Why does `s[0] = "X"` not change the string?
options: Strings are immutable; every operation returns a new string
Index assignment needs the charAt setter
It only fails under strict mode
It does change it, but the change is not visible until reassignment
quiz.explanation: There is no in-place mutation for strings. Building a result means concatenating or joining an array.

quiz.question: `"  hi  ".trim().length` is…
quiz.explanation: `trim` removes leading and trailing whitespace, leaving the two characters of "hi".

quiz.question: What does `"a,b,,c".split(",")` produce?
options: 4 items, one of them an empty string
4 items, the empty replaced with undefined
quiz.explanation: `split` keeps empty pieces. Filter them out yourself when consecutive separators are possible — a classic source of off-by-one word counts.

quiz.question: How do you compare two strings for sort order?
options: a.localeCompare(b), which returns a negative/zero/positive number
quiz.explanation: `localeCompare` is the comparator-shaped API. Subtraction on strings gives NaN, and there is no compareTo or equals in JavaScript.

exam.title: Title case and initials
exam.prompt: The input is a line of lowercase words. Print the line in Title Case, then the initials joined and uppercased, then the length of the longest word.
exam.hint: Strings are immutable, so build the capitalised word from w[0] plus w.slice(1).

weeks.title: Functions & Parameters
weeks.goal: Write functions with precise signatures — optional, default and rest parameters.

problems.note: A pure function with one parameter.
Branch inside a function and return early.
A function returning a union of possibilities.

weeks.project: Write a `format.ts` exporting `formatMoney(cents, options?)` where options may set a currency symbol and whether to show decimals — defaults for both.

quiz.question: Where must an optional parameter appear?
options: First, so callers can omit the rest
quiz.explanation: Positional arguments are matched left to right, so a required parameter can never follow an optional one.

quiz.question: What is the type of `x` in `function f(x = 5)`?
quiz.explanation: The default supplies the inferred type, and the parameter is optional from the caller's side but never undefined inside the body.

quiz.question: How is a rest parameter typed?
options: As a tuple of unknown length
quiz.explanation: `...items: number[]` collects the remaining arguments into a real array, which must be the last parameter.

quiz.question: What does a function declared to return `void` promise?
options: That callers should ignore whatever it returns
That it returns undefined and nothing else
quiz.explanation: `void` means the return value is not meaningful — which is why a `() => void` slot accepts a function that happens to return something. `never` is the type for functions that do not return at all.

quiz.question: What does the `?` in `function f(x?: number)` mean for the body?
options: x has type number | undefined and must be narrowed before use
x is always present at runtime
x can be passed in any position
quiz.explanation: Optional means possibly-undefined inside the function. A default value is what removes the undefined; `?` alone does not.

quiz.question: Why can a `() => void` slot accept `() => number`?
options: void means the return value is not meaningful, so returning something is allowed
It cannot — that is an error
quiz.explanation: This asymmetry is deliberate: it lets `arr.forEach(x => arr2.push(x))` type-check even though push returns a number.

exam.title: Formatter with options
exam.prompt: The input is `value width pad` where `pad` may be the word `none`. Write `format(value, width?, pad?)` with `width` defaulting to 8 and `pad` to `.`, returning the value right-aligned to that width. Print `format` applied to the input, then `format(value)` using both defaults.
exam.hint: Passing `undefined` for an optional parameter uses its default — which is exactly why `none` maps to undefined rather than an empty string.

weeks.title: Higher-Order Functions
weeks.goal: Pass and return functions, and read the types that describe them.

problems.note: Two passes, or one reduce and one filter.
A predicate handed to a counting helper.

weeks.project: Write a `pipeline.ts` with a `pipe` helper, then use it to build a text-cleaning pipeline from four small transforms.

quiz.question: What is the type of `const add = (a: number) => (b: number) => a + b`?
quiz.explanation: `add(1)` returns another function, so the return type is itself a function type. Only `add(1)(2)` gives a number.

quiz.question: Why does `["a"].map((s) => s.length)` type-check when map passes three arguments?
options: A function may declare fewer parameters than the signature offers
TypeScript infers the missing parameters as any
quiz.explanation: Assignability allows fewer parameters, never more — the callback simply ignores arguments it did not declare.

quiz.question: What does a closure capture?
options: The variable itself, so later changes to it are visible
A snapshot of the value at creation time
Nothing; parameters must be passed explicitly
quiz.explanation: Closures capture bindings, not values. This is why a `var` in a loop famously yields the final value while a `let` gives one binding per iteration.

quiz.question: Why are arrow functions the default for callbacks?
options: They inherit `this` from the enclosing scope instead of rebinding it
They cannot be passed to higher-order functions otherwise
They allow default parameters, which function expressions do not
quiz.explanation: A non-arrow callback gets its own `this`, which is almost never the object you meant — the classic source of `undefined is not a function` inside a method.

quiz.question: What is the type of `const add = (a: number) => (b: number) => a + b;`?
quiz.explanation: Calling `add(1)` hands back another function, so the return type is itself a function type. Only `add(1)(2)` produces a number.

quiz.question: Why does `['a','b'].map((s) => s.length)` type-check even though `map` passes three arguments to its callback?
options: A function may ignore trailing parameters it does not declare
The extra arguments are silently dropped at runtime only
TypeScript infers the missing parameters as any
quiz.explanation: Function assignability allows FEWER parameters than the target signature — the caller simply passes arguments the callback ignores. Declaring MORE than the signature offers is the error.

quiz.question: In `const shout = pipe<string>(f, g)`, what does `pipe` need to guarantee about `f` and `g`?
options: Both must be (x: string) => string so the output of one feeds the next
f must return the argument type of g, which can differ from string
Neither — pipe erases the types at runtime
quiz.explanation: This `pipe` is typed as `Array<(x: T) => T>`, so every stage takes and returns the SAME T. A pipeline that changes types between stages needs overloads or a more elaborate generic.

exam.title: Compose a text pipeline
exam.prompt: The input is a line of words. Build a `pipe` helper that composes `(s: string) => string` transforms left to right, then apply: trim, collapse runs of spaces to one, uppercase. Print the result, then the number of words in it.
exam.hint: pipe returns a function; reduce threads the value through each transform in order.

weeks.title: Arrays & Array Methods
weeks.goal: Use the array toolkit fluently and know which methods mutate.

problems.note: Math.max with a spread, or a scan.

weeks.project: Write a `table.ts` that reads CSV-ish lines and prints a summary: row count, per-column sums for numeric columns, and the widest value in each column.

quiz.question: Which of these MUTATES the array it is called on?
quiz.explanation: `sort` and `reverse` sort in place and return the same array — copy first with `[...arr].sort()` when the original matters.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `slice` and `splice`?
options: slice copies a range; splice removes or inserts in place
quiz.explanation: `slice` is non-destructive and returns a new array. `splice` edits the original and returns what it removed.

quiz.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].reduce((a, b) => a + b)` return without an initial value?
options: 6, using the first element as the seed
quiz.explanation: Without a seed the first element is used and iteration starts at index 1 — which throws on an EMPTY array, the reason to pass an explicit initial value.

quiz.question: What is a tuple type `[string, number]`?
options: A fixed-length array with a type per position
A union of string and number
An array that can hold either type in any position
quiz.explanation: Tuples fix both the length and the type at each index, which is what makes destructuring them type-safe.

quiz.question: What does `[10, 9, 1].sort()` return without a comparator?
quiz.explanation: The default sort converts to strings, so "10" sorts before "9". Numeric sorts always need `(a, b) => a - b`.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `find` and `filter`?
options: find returns the first match or undefined; filter returns an array of all matches
filter stops at the first match
quiz.explanation: `find` gives `T | undefined`, so its result needs a check before use — the type is telling you the search can fail.

exam.title: Array statistics
exam.prompt: The input is a line of numbers. Print, one per line: the sum, the maximum, the count of values above the mean, and the numbers sorted descending joined by spaces — without mutating the original order for the earlier answers.
exam.hint: sort mutates — copy with [...nums] first, and pass a numeric comparator or you get lexicographic order.

weeks.title: Destructuring, Objects & JSON
weeks.goal: Pull data apart cleanly, and cross the untyped JSON boundary safely.

problems.note: A frequency object, then a second pass.
Build structured output from a scan.

weeks.project: Write a `config.ts` that reads a JSON object from stdin, destructures the fields it needs with defaults, and prints a normalised summary.

quiz.question: What type does `JSON.parse(text)` return?
options: any — it is an unchecked boundary you should narrow immediately
quiz.explanation: `JSON.parse` is typed `any`, which quietly disables checking downstream. Assign it to `unknown` and validate with a type guard.

quiz.question: What does `const { a = 1 } = obj` do when `obj.a` is `null`?
options: Leaves a as null — defaults apply only to undefined
quiz.explanation: Destructuring defaults trigger on `undefined` only, exactly like parameter defaults. `null` is a real value and passes through.

quiz.question: What does the spread `{ ...a, ...b }` do on conflicting keys?
options: b wins, because later spreads overwrite earlier ones
quiz.explanation: Spread is a shallow, left-to-right copy. Nested objects are shared by reference, not cloned.

quiz.question: How do you rename while destructuring?
quiz.explanation: The colon form binds the property `a` to a new local name. The `as` spelling is for imports, not destructuring.

quiz.question: What does `const { a, ...rest } = obj` put in `rest`?
options: A new object with every own property except a
An array of the remaining values
Only the properties declared after a
quiz.explanation: Rest in a destructuring pattern builds a fresh shallow object. Nested values are still shared by reference.

quiz.question: `JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: 1 })` produces…
quiz.explanation: undefined, functions and symbols are omitted from objects (and become null inside arrays) — a routine source of fields vanishing over the wire.

exam.title: Merge JSON records
exam.prompt: The input is `n` then `n` lines of JSON objects with a `name` and optional `tags` array. Merge them into one record per name (later `tags` append, duplicates dropped) and print `name: tag1,tag2` per name in alphabetical order, tags sorted.
exam.hint: Destructure with a default for the optional tags, and use a Set per name so duplicates collapse.

weeks.title: Maps, Sets & Hashing
weeks.goal: Reach for the right keyed collection, and use it to turn O(n²) into O(n).

problems.note: A Set turns a sort into a linear scan.

weeks.project: Write an `index.ts` that reads lines of `word document` and builds an inverted index, then answers lookup queries from stdin.

quiz.question: When should you use a `Map` rather than a plain object?
options: When keys are not strings, insertion order matters, or you add and remove often
Always — objects are deprecated as dictionaries
Only when the keys are numbers
quiz.explanation: Objects coerce keys to strings and carry a prototype. `Map` takes any key type, preserves insertion order and has a real `size`.

quiz.question: What does `set.add(x)` return when `x` is already present?
options: The set itself — but `has` is how you test membership
quiz.explanation: `Set.add` returns the set for chaining. It is `Map.set` and `Set.add` returning the collection that makes the 'test and insert' idiom need a separate `has`.

quiz.question: Two distinct objects with identical contents used as Map keys…
options: Are two different keys, because Map compares by reference
Are compared structurally like TypeScript types
quiz.explanation: `Map` uses SameValueZero, which is reference identity for objects. Key by a primitive derived from the object when you want value semantics.

quiz.question: How do you iterate a Map's key/value pairs?
quiz.explanation: A Map is iterable over `[key, value]` entries. `for...in` sees nothing, and `forEach` passes value FIRST, which trips people up.

quiz.question: What does `map.get(missingKey)` return?
quiz.explanation: Which is why `Map.get` is typed `V | undefined` and the result should be checked against undefined rather than tested for truthiness.

quiz.question: Why is a Set-based duplicate check O(n) rather than O(n²)?
options: Set membership is roughly constant time, so one pass suffices
It is not — Set lookup is linear
quiz.explanation: Hashing turns 'have I seen this?' into a constant-time question, which is the whole reason hashing shows up in so many linear-time solutions.

exam.title: Inverted index
exam.prompt: The input is `n` then `n` lines of `document word word ...`, then a final line of query words. For each query print `word: doc1 doc2` (documents in first-appearance order) or `word: -` if unseen.
exam.hint: A Map from word to a document list; guard against adding the same document twice.

tests.input:
2
d1 cat dog
d2 dog bird
dog cat fish
tests.output:
dog: d1 d2
cat: d1
fish: -

weeks.title: Unions, Aliases & Literal Types
weeks.goal: Model 'one of a fixed set' precisely instead of reaching for `string`.

problems.note: A state that must be one of three values.
A union in, a union out.
Formatting driven by a small fixed vocabulary.

weeks.project: Write a `state.ts` modelling a download as `"idle" | "loading" | "done" | "failed"`, with a transition function that rejects illegal moves.

quiz.question: What does `type Status = "on" | "off"` buy you over `string`?
options: Only the two literals are assignable, and editors can complete them
It is stored more compactly at runtime
quiz.explanation: A literal union makes the illegal values unrepresentable at compile time. It has no runtime existence at all.

quiz.question: Which is true of `type` versus `interface`?
options: Interfaces merge across declarations; type aliases can express unions
Only type aliases can be extended
quiz.explanation: Both describe object shapes and both can be extended. Declaration merging is interface-only; unions, tuples and mapped types need a `type`.

quiz.question: What does `as const` do to `const dirs = ["up", "down"]`?
options: Makes it a readonly tuple of literal types instead of string[]
Makes the variable non-reassignable, which const already did
quiz.explanation: `as const` stops the widening from `"up"` to `string`, which is what lets `(typeof dirs)[number]` produce a useful union.

quiz.question: Why does this track avoid `enum`?
options: A literal union plus `as const` gives the same safety with no runtime object
enum cannot be used with switch
quiz.explanation: `enum` emits a real runtime object and has surprising numeric-enum behaviour. A string-literal union is erased entirely and narrows better.

quiz.question: What is the type of `"on"` in `const s = "on"` versus `let s = "on"`?
quiz.explanation: A `let` binding can be reassigned, so its type widens. This widening is exactly what `as const` prevents on object and array literals.

quiz.question: Can a `type` alias be used before it is declared?
options: Yes — type declarations are hoisted for the checker
No, they must be declared first
quiz.explanation: Type declarations are not statements with runtime order, so ordering is free. Recursive and mutually-recursive types depend on this.

exam.title: Traffic light machine
exam.prompt: States are `red`, `green`, `amber` and cycle red → green → amber → red. The input is a start state then a number of ticks. Print the state after each tick, one per line.
exam.hint: A Record keyed by the literal union is both the transition table and the proof that every state has a successor.

weeks.title: Narrowing & Type Guards
weeks.goal: Prove to the compiler what a value is — with built-in narrowing and your own predicates.

problems.note: A shape check expressed as a sequence of guards.

weeks.project: Write a `validate.ts` that reads JSON lines and keeps only those matching a `Person` shape, using a type predicate you wrote yourself.

quiz.question: What narrows `x: string | number` inside `if (typeof x === "string")`?
options: typeof narrowing, which the compiler understands natively
quiz.explanation: `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, equality against literals and truthiness checks are all built-in narrowing forms.

quiz.question: Why does `function isPerson(x: unknown): boolean` fail to narrow?
options: Only an `x is Person` return type carries narrowing information
boolean is not allowed as a return type
The parameter must be typed any
It does narrow, but only inside the function
quiz.explanation: A plain boolean tells the compiler nothing about the relationship between the result and the argument. The predicate form is what creates it.

quiz.question: `function isPerson(x: unknown): x is Person { return true; }` — the compiler…
options: Accepts it; predicates are unchecked promises
Rejects it as an unsound predicate
Narrows to unknown as a fallback
quiz.explanation: The body is never verified against the claim, which is exactly why a predicate should check every field it asserts.

quiz.question: What does `asserts x is string` do?
options: Narrows for the rest of the scope by throwing when the check fails
Returns a boolean you branch on
Is a synonym for `x is string`
quiz.explanation: An assertion function makes a demand rather than asking a question — control continues past it only when the value really is that type.

quiz.question: What changes if you write `function isPerson(x: unknown): boolean` instead of `: x is Person`?
options: The function still runs but no longer narrows x at the call site
x is narrowed to any instead of Person
quiz.explanation: Only the `x is T` return type carries narrowing information. With `: boolean` the compiler learns nothing from the `if`, so `x` stays `unknown` inside it.

quiz.question: `function isPerson(x: unknown): x is Person { return true; }` — what does TypeScript do?
options: Accepts it; the compiler trusts the predicate without verifying the body
Errors, because the body does not check any Person fields
Narrows to unknown instead, as a safety fallback
quiz.explanation: A type predicate is an unchecked promise. This is exactly why a predicate should test every field it claims — a sloppy one puts a hole straight through the type system.

quiz.question: What distinguishes `asserts x is string` from `x is string`?
options: The assertion narrows for the rest of the scope by throwing on failure, rather than returning a boolean to test
The assertion works on primitives only
The assertion is checked at runtime by TypeScript
There is no difference other than spelling
quiz.explanation: A predicate answers a question you branch on; an assertion function makes a demand — control only continues past the call when the value really is that type.

exam.title: Validate a batch of records
exam.prompt: The input is `n` then `n` JSON lines. A record is valid when it is an object with a string `id` of length 3+ and a number `score` between 0 and 100. Write a type predicate. Print `ok <id>` or `bad` per line, then the mean score of the valid ones rounded down (or `0` if none).
exam.hint: Reject non-objects and null first, then check every field the predicate claims — the compiler will not do it for you.

weeks.title: Discriminated Unions
weeks.goal: Model variants with a shared tag, and let the compiler prove you handled all of them.
weeks.project: Write an `interpreter.ts` for a tiny stack language (`push n`, `add`, `dup`, `print`) modelled as a discriminated union, with a `never` exhaustiveness check.

quiz.question: Why must the discriminant be a literal type?
options: Only distinct literals let narrowing rule out the other union members
TypeScript forbids string properties in unions
It is required for JSON serialization
quiz.explanation: Narrowing works by elimination. With `kind: string` both members still match, so nothing is excluded.

quiz.question: You add a new variant. What does `const exhaustive: never = value` in the default branch do?
options: Errors in every switch that has not handled the new variant
Narrows the new variant to never
quiz.explanation: That is the whole point: the compiler walks you to every place that now needs a case, instead of failing silently in production.

quiz.question: What is the advantage over one object with all fields optional?
options: Each branch guarantees which fields exist, removing runtime undefined checks
quiz.explanation: All-optional fields make every impossible combination representable and every access a guard. The tag makes the illegal states unrepresentable.

quiz.question: Does `if (s.kind === "circle")` narrow as well as `switch`?
options: Yes — equality against a literal is a narrowing form
quiz.explanation: Both narrow identically. An `else if` chain still wants a final `never` check to stay exhaustive.

quiz.question: Why must the discriminant be a literal type rather than `string`?
options: Only distinct literal types let the compiler rule out the other union members
String discriminants are slower at runtime
TypeScript forbids string-typed properties in unions
Literal types are required for JSON serialization
quiz.explanation: Narrowing works by elimination: `kind === \"circle\"` can only exclude the rect member if that member's `kind` is the literal `\"rect\"`. With `kind: string` both members still match.

quiz.question: You add a `{ kind: "triangle"; b: number; h: number }` member. What does the `const exhaustive: never = s` line do?
options: It becomes a compile error in every switch that has not handled the new kind
It silently accepts the new member
It throws at runtime when a triangle arrives
It narrows the triangle to never so the switch keeps working
quiz.explanation: That is the point of the pattern: `s` in `default` is now the triangle member, which is not assignable to `never`, so the compiler walks you to every place that needs a new case.

quiz.question: Which is the real advantage of a tagged union over one object with all fields optional?
options: Each branch statically guarantees which fields exist, removing the undefined checks
It uses less memory at runtime
It allows more than one field to be required
It survives JSON.stringify, which optional fields do not
quiz.explanation: With all-optional fields every access needs a runtime guard and the compiler cannot tell a circle from a rect. The tag makes the impossible combinations unrepresentable.

quiz.question: `const nums = [3, 1, 2]; const sorted = nums.sort();` — what is `nums` afterwards?
options: [1, 2, 3] — sort mutates, and sorted is the same array
[1, 2, 3], but sorted is a separate array

quiz.question: Which pair of values makes `a ?? b` and `a || b` disagree?
quiz.explanation: `0` is falsy but not nullish, so `||` returns 5 while `??` returns 0. This is the bug `??` was introduced to prevent.

quiz.question: You have `x: unknown` from JSON.parse. What is the safest next step?

Use `any` so the checks stop complaining

quiz.question: What single flag most changes what a type annotation means?

quiz.question: `const a = [1,2]; const b = a; b.push(3);` — what is `a.length`?

quiz.question: Which is the safest way to handle a value of type `unknown`?

Annotate the variable with the expected type
Assign it to an any-typed variable
quiz.explanation: Casts and annotations both assert without verifying. Only a real runtime check makes the resulting type honest.

weeks.goal: Handle absence explicitly, and know which flag is catching you.

problems.note: Boundary conditions on an index scan.

weeks.project: Take your Week 8 config reader and turn on `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in your head: rewrite every index access to handle `undefined` honestly.

quiz.question: With `strictNullChecks` on, what does `string` mean?
options: A string — absence must be written as string | null or string | undefined
The same as before; the flag only affects parameters
quiz.explanation: The flag is what makes annotations mean what they say. Off, every type quietly includes the nullish values.

quiz.question: What does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` change?
options: arr[i] becomes T | undefined, reflecting that the index may be out of range
It throws at runtime on a bad index
quiz.explanation: It tells the truth about indexing. Not part of `strict`, usually the most disruptive flag to adopt — and the most valuable.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `a?.b` and `a!.b`?
options: ?. short-circuits to undefined; !. asserts a is non-null and checks nothing
!. throws a helpful error when a is null
quiz.explanation: The non-null assertion is a promise, not a check. If it is wrong you get a plain runtime TypeError with no extra context.

quiz.question: Why prefer `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore`?
options: It errors once the problem is fixed, so the suppression cannot outlive its reason
quiz.explanation: `@ts-ignore` hides whatever the next line does, forever. `@ts-expect-error` fails when there is nothing left to suppress.

quiz.question: What does `strictNullChecks` change about the meaning of `string`?
options: With it on, `string` excludes null and undefined — absence must be written explicitly
quiz.explanation: With the flag off, every type silently includes null and undefined, so no annotation can be trusted. It is the flag the rest of the type system's usefulness rests on.

quiz.question: What does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` do?
options: Gives `arr[i]` the type `T | undefined`, reflecting that the index may be out of range
Throws at runtime on an out-of-range index
Requires every array access to use .at()
quiz.explanation: It tells the truth about indexing. It is not part of `strict`, and it is usually the most disruptive flag to enable in an existing codebase — and the most valuable.

weeks.title: Assertions, satisfies & Structural Typing
weeks.goal: Understand what the compiler compares, and the two very different ways to override it.

problems.note: Build to an interface without inheriting from one.

weeks.project: Write a `routes.ts` that declares a route table with `satisfies`, derives the route-name union from it, and exposes a lookup that rejects unknown names.

quiz.question: What does `satisfies` do that an annotation does not?
options: Checks the value against the type while keeping its narrower inferred type
Widens the value to the given type
quiz.explanation: An annotation replaces the inferred type; `satisfies` only validates against it, so literal keys and tuple shapes survive.

quiz.question: Why is `const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, label: "h" }` an error when assigning the same object via a variable is not?
options: The excess property check applies only to fresh object literals assigned directly
Both are errors, reported at different times
quiz.explanation: The literal form is where typos live, so TypeScript checks it. Widening through a variable falls back to ordinary structural assignability.

quiz.question: Two unrelated aliases with identical members — is one assignable to the other?
options: Yes; structural typing compares shapes, not names
No; they are distinct named types
Only if one extends the other
quiz.explanation: Nothing links them by name, but their members match. This is the core difference from Java's nominal `implements`.

quiz.question: What makes a class partly nominal?
options: private or protected members, which only match the declaring class
quiz.explanation: Private members are tied to their declaration, so two identical-looking classes are not interchangeable — the one nominal corner of the system.

quiz.question: What does `satisfies` do that a type annotation does not?
options: It validates the value against the type while keeping the value's own narrower inferred type
It validates the value at runtime
It widens the value to the given type
quiz.explanation: An annotation replaces the inferred type; `satisfies` only checks against it. That is how you keep literal key and tuple information while still enforcing a contract.

quiz.question: With `const routes = { home: "/" } satisfies Record<string, string>`, what is `keyof typeof routes`?
quiz.explanation: The inferred object type is preserved, so its keys are the literal union of what was actually written. With a plain `Record<string, string>` annotation it would have been `string`.

quiz.question: Does `satisfies` help validate JSON arriving from a network call?
options: No — it is erased at compile time and checks nothing at runtime
Yes, it throws when the shape does not match
Yes, but only in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Like every type-level construct it disappears before the code runs. Runtime data still needs a type predicate or a schema validator.

quiz.question: `const bad: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, label: "home" };` errors, but assigning the same object through a variable does not. Why?
options: The excess property check only applies to fresh object literals assigned directly
Variables are always typed as any
The variable version is also an error, just reported later
label is a reserved property name
quiz.explanation: TypeScript treats a directly-assigned literal as a place where extra keys are almost certainly typos, so it checks them. Once the object is widened into a variable, ordinary structural assignability applies.

quiz.question: Two unrelated aliases `type A = { id: number }` and `type B = { id: number }`. Is `const b: B = someA;` legal?
options: Yes — structural typing compares shapes, not declaration names
No — they are different named types
Only when both are interfaces rather than type aliases
quiz.explanation: Nothing links A and B by name, but they have identical members, so each is assignable to the other. This is the core difference from Java's nominal `implements`.

quiz.question: What makes a class NOT purely structural in TypeScript?
options: Having private or protected members, which only match members from the same declaration
quiz.explanation: Private and protected members are tied to their declaring class, so two classes with identical-looking private fields are not interchangeable — the one nominal corner of the type system.

exam.title: Route table with satisfies
exam.prompt: Declare a route table (`home` → `/`, `about` → `/about`, `docs` → `/docs`) checked with `satisfies Record<string, string>`, derive the name union from it, and look up each of the `n` requested names. Print the path or `404`, then the number of routes.
exam.hint: `satisfies` keeps the keys literal, so `keyof typeof routes` is the three names rather than plain string.

weeks.title: Branded Types & Immutability
weeks.goal: Make validated values a type, and stop accidental mutation at the boundary.

problems.note: Build a new array rather than editing in place.
Compare the in-place and copying solutions honestly.

weeks.project: Write an `ids.ts` with branded `UserId` and `OrderId`, validating parsers for both, and a `readonly` lookup table that cannot be mutated by callers.

quiz.question: What does a brand cost at runtime?
options: Nothing — the intersection is erased and the value stays a plain string
A hidden property on each value
quiz.explanation: That is the appeal over a wrapper class: nominal safety with zero runtime representation.

quiz.question: Why should exactly one function apply the `as UserId` cast?
options: It concentrates the unchecked assertion in one validated place
TypeScript allows one cast per type
quiz.explanation: A brand is only as trustworthy as the assertions that create it. Scattered casts mean the type proves nothing.

quiz.question: What does `readonly string[]` prevent?
options: Calling mutating methods and assigning to indices
quiz.explanation: It is a compile-time restriction on the array's own operations. `const` only stops rebinding the variable.

quiz.question: Does `Object.freeze` give you a deeply immutable object?
options: No — it is shallow; nested objects remain mutable
quiz.explanation: Freezing one level is the runtime counterpart to `Readonly<T>`, which is also shallow. Deep immutability needs a recursive helper.

quiz.question: Why should the constructor function be the ONLY place that writes `as UserId`?
options: It concentrates the unchecked assertion in one validated spot, so the type genuinely implies the invariant
TypeScript only allows one cast per type
Casting elsewhere is a runtime error
The compiler tracks how many casts a program contains
quiz.explanation: The brand is only as trustworthy as the assertions that create it. Scattering casts around means the type no longer proves anything.

quiz.question: How can you check at runtime whether a value is a `UserId`?
options: You cannot directly — you must re-run the validation the constructor performs
quiz.explanation: Since the brand is erased there is nothing to inspect. Runtime questions about a branded value always come back to re-checking the underlying data.

exam.title: Branded money
exam.prompt: Brand `Cents` and `Dollars`. The input is `n` then `n` amounts in cents. Print the running total in cents after each, then the final total in dollars (cents / 100). Only a validating constructor may produce a branded value; reject negatives by printing `invalid` for that line and skipping it.
exam.hint: Return `Cents | null` from the constructor so the caller must handle bad input; the cast inside it is the single place the brand is applied.

weeks.title: Composition & Utility Types
weeks.goal: Build types out of other types instead of restating them.

problems.note: Sort, then fold — with a well-typed interval.
A variant of the same model.
The simplest form of the pattern.

weeks.project: Model a `Task` type, then derive `TaskDraft` (no id), `TaskPatch` (all optional) and `TaskSummary` (a few fields) with `Omit`, `Partial` and `Pick` rather than three hand-written types.

quiz.question: What does `Omit<T, K>` do?
options: Produces T without the properties named in K
Makes the properties in K optional
Keeps only the properties in K
quiz.explanation: `Pick` keeps, `Omit` removes. `Omit` is defined in terms of `Pick` and `Exclude`.

quiz.question: How do you combine two object types?
options: An intersection: A & B, or interface B extends A
quiz.explanation: An intersection requires BOTH sets of members. A union means 'one or the other', which is the opposite of combining.

quiz.question: What is `Record<string, number>`?
options: An object type with string keys and number values
A tuple of a string and a number
A union of string and number
quiz.explanation: `Record` is a mapped type: `{ [P in K]: V }`. Note that a string-keyed Record loses literal key checking.

quiz.question: `Partial<T>` makes every property optional. What is its inverse?
quiz.explanation: `Required<T>` is `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` — the `-?` strips the optional modifier the source type had.

quiz.question: What does `A & B` mean for two object types?
options: A value must satisfy BOTH — it has all members of A and of B
A value must satisfy either one
quiz.explanation: Intersection combines requirements. It is unions that mean 'one or the other', which is the opposite of what people first expect from the & symbol.

quiz.question: What is `Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "b">`?
quiz.explanation: `Exclude` filters a union with a distributive conditional type. `Omit` is the object-level cousin, built from Exclude and Pick.

exam.title: Merge intervals
exam.prompt: The input is `n` then `n` lines of `start end`. Merge every overlapping or touching interval and print the merged ones as `start end`, one per line sorted by start, then how many intervals were absorbed (input count minus output count).
exam.hint: Sort by start, then either extend the last merged interval or push a copy of the current one.

weeks.title: Generics & Constraints
weeks.goal: Write one implementation that keeps every caller's exact type.

problems.note: A function whose signature is the interesting part.

weeks.project: Write a `collections.ts` exporting generic `unique`, `groupBy`, `partition` and `sortBy` helpers, each preserving the input's element type.

quiz.question: Why is `<T extends { length: number }>` better than a plain `{ length: number }` parameter?
options: The generic returns the caller's exact type instead of collapsing it
The non-generic form does not compile
quiz.explanation: Both accept the same arguments. The difference is on the way out — the generic hands back `string` for strings.

quiz.question: In `get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, what is `T[K]`?
options: An indexed access type — the type of the property named K
An array of T indexed by K
quiz.explanation: It looks up a property type by name, which is how one signature returns `string` for one key and `number` for another.

quiz.question: What does a type-parameter default like `<T = string>` do?
options: Supplies T only when inference has nothing to work from
quiz.explanation: It is not a value default. `makeBox(1)` still infers `number`; the default matters when no argument drives inference.

quiz.question: When is a generic the WRONG tool?
options: When the body never uses T — a plain parameter type is clearer
When there is more than one type parameter
quiz.explanation: A type parameter used once and never related to anything else adds noise without adding a guarantee.

quiz.question: Why is `function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T` better than `function longest(a: { length: number }, b: { length: number }): { length: number }`?
options: The generic returns the caller's exact type instead of collapsing it to { length: number }
The generic is faster at runtime
The non-generic version does not compile
quiz.explanation: Both accept the same arguments. The difference is on the way out: the generic hands back `string` for strings, while the plain signature loses everything except `.length`.

quiz.question: In `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, what is `T[K]`?
options: An indexed access type — the type of the property named K on T
An array of T indexed by K
quiz.explanation: `T[K]` looks up a property type by name, which is what lets one signature return `string` for `\"name\"` and `number` for `\"age\"`.

quiz.question: What does the default in `function makeBox<T = string>(value: T)` actually do?
options: It supplies T only when inference has nothing to infer from
It makes the value parameter optional
It coerces the argument to string
quiz.explanation: A type-parameter default is not a value default. `makeBox(1)` still infers `T = number`; the default matters for cases like `const b: Box = ...` where no argument drives inference.

exam.title: Generic collection helpers
exam.prompt: Write generic `unique`, `groupBy` and `sortBy`. The input is `n` then `n` lines of `category value`. Print each category in alphabetical order as `category: v1 v2` with its values sorted numerically ascending and duplicates removed, then the number of categories.
exam.hint: `K extends keyof T` is what keeps the Map keyed by the field's real type instead of collapsing to string.

weeks.title: keyof, typeof & Indexed Access
weeks.goal: Derive types from values so one source of truth drives both.

problems.note: A keyed store with a typed accessor.

weeks.project: Write a `settings.ts` where one `as const` object defines the defaults, and every getter, setter and key union is derived from it — adding a setting should require exactly one edit.

quiz.question: What is `(typeof levels)[number]` when `const levels = ["a", "b"] as const`?
quiz.explanation: `as const` keeps the elements literal, and indexing the tuple type by `number` unions them — the standard derive-a-union idiom.

quiz.question: Drop the `as const`. What does it become?
quiz.explanation: The array widens to `string[]`, so the literal information is gone before the type-level trick can use it.

quiz.question: How does type-position `typeof` differ from the runtime operator?
options: It lifts a value into a type; the runtime one returns a string when executed
The type one works on classes only
quiz.explanation: They share a keyword and nothing else. One computes a type, the other is a runtime check that happens to narrow.

quiz.question: What is `keyof Record<string, number>`?
quiz.explanation: `keyof` on an index signature gives the index type, and numeric keys are also valid string keys — which is why it includes `number`.

quiz.question: Drop the `as const`. What does `(typeof levels)[number]` become?
quiz.explanation: Without `as const` the array widens to `string[]`, so indexing it by number yields `string` — the literal information is gone before the type-level trick can use it.

quiz.question: How does the type-position `typeof` differ from the runtime `typeof` operator?
options: The type-position one lifts a value into a type; the runtime one returns a string at execution time
They are the same operator used in two places
The type-position one only works on classes
The runtime one is removed by the compiler
quiz.explanation: They share a keyword and nothing else. `type S = typeof settings` computes a type; `typeof x === \"string\"` is a runtime check that happens to also narrow.

exam.title: Settings from one source of truth
exam.prompt: Declare a defaults object, derive `Setting` with `keyof typeof`, and write a `read<K extends Setting>` returning `Profile[K]`. Defaults are `theme: "dark"`, `size: 14`, `wrap: true`. The input is `n` then `n` setting names. Print each value, or `unknown`, then the boolean-valued keys in alphabetical order.
exam.hint: One object drives the values, the key union and the getter's return type — adding a setting should need exactly one edit.

weeks.title: Mapped Types
weeks.goal: Transform every property of a type at once — and build what the type describes.

problems.note: A container described by a derived type.

weeks.project: Reimplement `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick` and `Omit` from scratch in a `utils.d.ts`, then check each against the built-in with a type-level test.

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` produce?
options: Every property made required — the built-in Required<T>
A union of T's property types
quiz.explanation: The `-` prefix strips a modifier the source had. `-readonly` does the same for readonly.

quiz.question: In an `as` clause, what happens to a key mapped to `never`?
options: The property is removed — this is how Omit works
quiz.explanation: Key remapping to `never` drops the entry, which is the mechanism behind every filtering utility type.

quiz.question: You define `Getters<T>` renaming keys to getName/getAge. What exists at runtime?
options: Nothing — the type only describes an object you still have to build
The original object with extra prototype methods
quiz.explanation: Mapped types are erased like everything else in the type system. They describe an obligation your runtime code has to meet.

quiz.question: What is `keyof (A | B)`?
options: The keys A and B have in COMMON
quiz.explanation: Only shared keys are safe to access on a value that might be either — a frequent surprise when mapping over a union.

quiz.question: In a mapped type's `as` clause, what happens to a key you map to `never`?
options: The property is removed from the result — this is how Omit works
quiz.explanation: Key remapping to `never` drops the entry entirely, which is exactly the mechanism behind filtering utilities like `Omit`.

quiz.question: You define `type Getters<T>` that renames keys to `getName`, `getAge`. What exists at runtime?
options: Nothing — you must still build the object yourself; the type only describes it
An object with those methods, generated by the compiler
A proxy that forwards property access
The original object with extra prototype methods
quiz.explanation: Mapped types are erased like every other type. They describe the shape your runtime code is obliged to produce, usually ending in a cast where the loop finishes.

exam.title: Build what the mapped type describes
exam.prompt: `Getters<T>` renames each key to `getX` returning that property's type. The input is a name. Build the getters object at runtime for `{ name, size: 5 }`, then print `getName()`, `getSize()`, and the getter keys sorted and comma-joined.
exam.hint: The mapped type is erased — the loop has to produce the renamed keys itself, and the cast at the end is where you assert it matched.

weeks.title: Conditional Types & infer
weeks.goal: Branch on types and pattern-match their structure.

problems.note: A hashing problem worth revisiting with better types.

weeks.project: Write a `types.ts` implementing `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, `Awaited` and `Exclude` yourself, with a comment on each explaining where `infer` binds.

quiz.question: What does `infer` do?
options: Binds a fresh type variable to whatever matched at that position
Declares a default for the type parameter
Converts a value into a type
quiz.explanation: `T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T` matches T against 'array of something' and names that something `U`.

quiz.question: `type NonNil<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T`. What is `NonNil<string | null>`?
quiz.explanation: T is naked, so the conditional distributes: `string` takes the else branch, `null` becomes `never`, and `never` vanishes from a union.

quiz.question: How do you STOP a conditional type distributing?
options: Wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y
quiz.explanation: Distribution needs a bare type parameter. Putting it in a tuple makes it non-naked, so the check runs once on the whole union.

quiz.question: What is `IsString<any>` for `type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no"`?
quiz.explanation: `any` is assignable to everything and nothing simultaneously, so a conditional over it resolves to the union of both branches.

quiz.question: What does `infer` do inside a conditional type?
options: Binds a fresh type variable to whatever type matched at that position
Forces TypeScript to re-infer the whole expression
Declares a default for the type parameter
Converts a value into a type
quiz.explanation: `T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T` matches T against 'array of something' and names that something `U` — pattern matching on the type's structure.

quiz.question: How do you stop a conditional type from distributing over a union?
options: Wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y
Use an interface instead of a type alias
quiz.explanation: Distribution requires a bare type parameter on the left. Putting it inside a tuple makes it non-naked, so the check runs once against the whole union.

exam.title: Unwrap and compact
exam.prompt: Write `Unwrap<T>` (element type of an array, else T) and `NonNil<T>` (drops null/undefined from a union). The input is a line of tokens where `-` means null. Print the first non-null token or `(none)`, then the compacted tokens space-separated or `(none)`, then how many were dropped.
exam.hint: Both types are erased, so each function ends in a cast — the type describes what the runtime branch is obliged to produce.

weeks.goal: Encode naming conventions in the type system, and describe unbounded data.

problems.note: A recursive structure with a recursive type.

weeks.project: Write an `events.ts` where the entity and action lists are `as const` arrays, the event-name type is a template literal over them, and a typed emitter rejects any name not in the catalogue.

quiz.question: How many members does `` `${"a" | "b"}-${"x" | "y" | "z"}` `` have?
quiz.explanation: Interpolating unions gives the cross product — 2 × 3. This growth is also why deeply nested templates can exhaust the compiler.

quiz.question: Where can `Capitalize<T>` be used?
options: Only inside template literal types — it is a compiler intrinsic
quiz.explanation: `Capitalize`, `Uppercase`, `Lowercase` and `Uncapitalize` live purely in the type system. Capitalizing a real string is still your own code.

quiz.question: Why is `type Bad = Bad | string` an error while `type Json = string | Json[]` is fine?
options: A recursive alias must go through an object, array or function
type aliases cannot be recursive at all
quiz.explanation: `Bad` refers to itself with nothing to defer into. Wrapping the recursion in `Json[]` gives the checker a structure to expand lazily.

quiz.question: What does `T extends readonly [unknown, ...infer Rest]` accomplish?
options: Peels the first tuple element and binds the rest, enabling recursion
Checks T is a readonly array
quiz.explanation: It is the type-level head/tail destructure — the shrinking step every recursive tuple algorithm needs.

quiz.question: How many members does `` type T = `${"a" | "b"}-${"x" | "y" | "z"}` `` have?
quiz.explanation: Interpolating unions produces the cross product — 2 × 3 = 6 literal types. This growth is also why deeply nested templates can blow the compiler's limits.

quiz.question: Why does `function toSize(v: number, u: Unit): Size { return `${v}${u}` as Size; }` need the cast?
options: A template built from a runtime `number` widens to `string`, which the compiler cannot prove matches the pattern
Casts are always required when returning template literals
Unit is a union, and unions cannot be interpolated
quiz.explanation: Type-level interpolation over `${number}` works on literal types. A runtime value produces an ordinary `string`, so you assert the invariant your code maintains.

quiz.question: In `type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K] }`, what is the base case?
options: A property whose type is not an object, which stops the recursion
quiz.explanation: The conditional decides at each property whether to recurse. Primitives take the else branch and terminate that path.

exam.title: Event catalogue
exam.prompt: Entities are `user`, `order`; actions are `created`, `updated`, `deleted`. Derive `EventName` as a template literal over `as const` arrays and build the catalogue at runtime. The input is `n` then `n` candidate names. Print `ok` or `bad` per name, then the catalogue size, then the names for `user` sorted.
exam.hint: The nested loops over the two as-const arrays produce exactly the six names the template literal type describes.

weeks.title: Classes & Encapsulation
weeks.goal: Use classes where they pay — real privacy, invariants and accessors.

problems.note: Two structures kept in step behind one interface.

weeks.project: Write an `account.ts` with a `BankAccount` class whose balance is `#private`, exposing `deposit`, `withdraw` (rejecting overdrafts) and a computed `balance` getter.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `#count` and `private count`?
options: `#` is enforced by the JavaScript engine; `private` is erased at compile time
`#` cannot be used in generic classes
quiz.explanation: A `private` field is visible to any JavaScript that ignores the types. A `#` field is genuinely inaccessible from outside the class.

quiz.question: Why do arrow-function class fields fix the `this` problem?
options: They capture `this` from the instance at construction rather than at call time
They are bound by the compiler
They cannot be detached from the object
quiz.explanation: Passing `obj.method` as a callback loses the receiver. An arrow field closes over `this` when the instance is built, so it travels with the function.

quiz.question: What does a `get` accessor let you do?
options: Expose a computed value through property syntax
quiz.explanation: Getters compute on access; `set` accessors are the ones that validate assignment. `readonly` is a separate modifier.

quiz.question: When should you NOT reach for a class?
options: When the thing is plain data with no invariant to protect
When there is more than one instance
quiz.explanation: Data with no behaviour is better as a plain object plus functions — it stays serializable and structurally typed.

quiz.question: Why does `const f = obj.method; f();` often break?
options: `this` is lost when the method is detached from its receiver
Methods cannot be assigned to variables
It only breaks in strict mode
quiz.explanation: A plain method call binds `this` from the call site. An arrow-function class field, or an explicit bind, keeps the receiver attached.

quiz.question: What does `readonly` on a class field prevent?
options: Mutating the object the field points at
quiz.explanation: It is a compile-time restriction on reassigning the field. The object it references can still be mutated freely.

exam.title: Bank account with invariants
exam.prompt: Write a `BankAccount` class with a `#balance`, a `deposit`, a `withdraw` that refuses overdrafts, and a `balance` getter. The input is `n` then `n` commands (`deposit n`, `withdraw n`). Print the balance after each command, printing `refused` instead when a withdrawal would overdraw, then the final balance.
exam.hint: The invariant lives inside the class: withdraw is the only path that reduces #balance, and it refuses rather than going negative.

weeks.title: Iterators, Generators & Generic Data Structures
weeks.goal: Produce values lazily and build containers that feel built-in.

problems.note: A container with an interface contract.

weeks.project: Write a `lazy.ts` with generator-based `range`, `map`, `filter`, `take` and `chunk`, then use them to process an infinite sequence without materialising it.

quiz.question: What happens the second time you iterate the same generator object?
options: Nothing is produced — it is exhausted after one pass
quiz.explanation: A generator holds its own position. Return a FUNCTION when callers may need to iterate more than once.

quiz.question: Why does `take(naturals(), 4)` terminate?
options: Generators are lazy — naturals only computes when take asks, and take stops asking
naturals is evaluated up to a default limit
quiz.explanation: Production is driven entirely by consumption. Spreading `naturals()` with no `take` really would hang.

quiz.question: Why type `pop()` as `T | undefined` rather than `T`?
options: An empty stack really returns undefined, and the type should say so
Generic methods cannot return a bare T
quiz.explanation: Typing it `T` hands the caller an `undefined` the compiler swears is a real value — exactly the bug types exist to prevent.

quiz.question: What does `yield*` do?
options: Delegates to another iterable, yielding all its values in place
Yields an array of the remaining values
quiz.explanation: It forwards every value from the inner iterable as if written inline — the standard way to compose generators.

quiz.question: What happens the second time you iterate the SAME generator object?
options: Nothing is produced — a generator object is exhausted after one pass
It yields the values in reverse
quiz.explanation: The generator holds its own position. If callers may iterate more than once, hand back a function that creates a fresh generator each time.

quiz.question: Why does `take(naturals(), 4)` terminate even though `naturals()` never ends?
options: Generators are lazy — naturals only computes a value when take asks, and take stops asking
TypeScript detects the infinite loop and bounds it
naturals() is evaluated eagerly up to a default limit
The spread operator caps at 1000 elements
quiz.explanation: Laziness is the point: production is driven entirely by consumption. Spreading `naturals()` directly, with no `take`, really would hang.

quiz.question: Why should `pop()` be typed `T | undefined` rather than `T`?
options: An empty stack really does return undefined, and the type should say so
Generic methods cannot return a bare T
undefined is required for iteration to work
quiz.explanation: Typing it as `T` is a lie that hands the caller an `undefined` the compiler swears is a real value — precisely the class of bug the type system exists to prevent.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `#items` and `private items`?
options: `#items` is private at runtime too; `private` is erased and the field is visible in JavaScript
`#items` cannot be used in a generic class
quiz.explanation: `#` is a real JavaScript private field enforced by the engine. `private` is a compile-time-only marker, so anything ignoring the types can still reach the value.

quiz.question: Why does a generic `SortedList<T>` take a comparator instead of constraining `T extends Comparable`?
options: T is erased at runtime, so ordering must be supplied as a function the class can call
Comparable does not exist in the TypeScript standard library
Constraints cannot be used on classes
Comparators are faster than interface dispatch
quiz.explanation: Both parts are true — there is no built-in Comparable — but the underlying reason is erasure: nothing about `T` survives to run, so the behaviour has to be passed in as a value.

exam.title: Lazy pipeline over an infinite source
exam.prompt: Write generators `naturals`, `filter`, `map` and `take`. The input is `count divisor`. Take the first `count` naturals divisible by `divisor`, square them, and print them space-separated (or `(none)`), then their sum. Nothing infinite may be materialised.
exam.hint: take must `return` the moment it has enough — that is what stops the infinite source being pulled forever.

weeks.title: Errors & Async
weeks.goal: Make failure visible in the type, and run async work concurrently on purpose.

problems.note: Time-ordered state with clear failure modes.
Incremental computation you could plausibly make async.

weeks.project: Write a `fetchAll.ts` that loads several simulated resources concurrently, races each against a timeout, and returns a `Result` per resource — no exception escapes.

quiz.question: Under `strict`, what type does `catch (e)` give `e`?
quiz.explanation: Any value can be thrown, so TypeScript refuses to assume `Error`. Narrow with `instanceof` before reading properties.

quiz.question: What makes `Result<T, E>` enforce handling?
options: It is a discriminated union — `value` only exists after checking `ok`
It throws if the error branch is ignored
quiz.explanation: On the failure branch there is no `value` property at all, so skipping the check is a type error rather than a runtime surprise.

quiz.question: What is the total time of `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne))` versus awaiting in a loop?
options: The maximum of the individual times, versus the sum
quiz.explanation: `.map` starts every promise before `all` waits, so they overlap. A loop starts each only after the previous resolves.

quiz.question: How does `Promise.race` differ from `Promise.any`?
options: race settles with the first to settle either way; any waits for the first SUCCESS
any is the async version of race
quiz.explanation: `race` is the timeout pattern precisely because an early rejection wins. `any` ignores rejections until every input has failed.

quiz.question: What makes `Result<T, E>` enforce error handling?
options: It is a discriminated union, so `value` is only reachable after checking `ok`
It throws if you ignore the error branch
E defaults to string, which cannot be ignored
quiz.explanation: The `ok` field is the discriminant. On the `false` branch there is no `value` property at all, so skipping the check is a type error rather than a runtime surprise.

quiz.question: When is throwing the better choice over returning a Result?
options: For bugs and unrecoverable invariant violations the caller cannot sensibly handle
quiz.explanation: Expected, recoverable failures belong in the return type. Genuinely exceptional situations — an impossible branch, a broken invariant — should unwind loudly.

quiz.question: What is the total time of `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne))` versus awaiting inside a loop?
options: The maximum of the individual times, versus the sum of them
The same — Promise.all is just syntax
Depends on the number of CPU cores
quiz.explanation: `.map` starts every promise before `all` waits, so they overlap. Awaiting inside a loop starts each one only after the previous resolves.

quiz.question: How does `Promise.allSettled` differ from `Promise.all` on failure?
options: It never rejects; every entry becomes a fulfilled/rejected record you inspect
It rejects only if every promise fails
It resolves with the successful values and silently drops failures
quiz.explanation: `allSettled` always resolves with one `PromiseSettledResult` per input. That last behaviour — dropping failures — is what `Promise.any` approximates, and it is not what allSettled does.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `Promise.race` and `Promise.any`?
options: race settles with the first promise to settle either way; any waits for the first SUCCESS
any is the async version of race
quiz.explanation: `race` is the timeout pattern precisely because an early rejection wins. `any` ignores rejections until all of them fail, then rejects with an AggregateError.

exam.title: Concurrent loads with a Result
exam.prompt: `load(id)` resolves to `id * 10` after `id` ms but rejects for a negative id. Run every id concurrently, convert each outcome to a `Result`, and print `id=value` or `id=failed` in input order, then the number that succeeded and their total, space-separated.
exam.hint: allSettled never rejects, so one bad id cannot lose the others; converting each entry to a Result makes the caller handle both branches.

weeks.title: Modules, Declarations & Capstone
weeks.goal: Structure a real project, describe the code you do not own, and prove the six months.

problems.note: The hardest design problem in the bank — take your time.

weeks.project: Capstone: build a small typed CLI as a multi-file project — a `Result`-based parser, a branded id type, a generic store with an iterator, an ambient declaration for one host global, and `strict` plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` clean.

quiz.question: What does a `.d.ts` file emit at build time?
options: Nothing — it only describes types the runtime is assumed to provide
A module that must be imported
quiz.explanation: Declaration files are pure description. Declaring something the runtime lacks gives a ReferenceError with no compile-time warning.

quiz.question: Why must module augmentation use `interface` rather than `type`?
options: Interfaces merge across declarations; type aliases cannot be reopened
type is illegal inside declare module
Interfaces are erased and types are not
quiz.explanation: Declaration merging is interface-only, and it is what lets you ADD a field to a library type instead of shadowing it.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a default export and a named export?
options: A default can be imported under any name, which makes it easy to rename inconsistently
A default is faster to load
A module may have several defaults
quiz.explanation: Named exports keep one canonical spelling across the codebase, which is why many style guides prefer them for anything but a single obvious entry point.

quiz.question: What does `import type { X } from "./x"` guarantee?
options: The import is erased entirely, so no runtime module dependency is created
X must be a type alias, not an interface
The module is loaded but unused
quiz.explanation: It makes the type-only intent explicit, avoiding a runtime import that a bundler would otherwise have to keep — the point of `verbatimModuleSyntax`.

quiz.question: Why does a file using `declare global` usually need `export {};`?
options: It forces the file to be a module, which `declare global` requires
It prevents the globals from leaking
It is a convention with no effect
quiz.explanation: A file with no imports or exports is a script, and its top-level declarations are already global — so `declare global` is only meaningful (and only legal) inside a module.

exam.title: Capstone: typed record store
exam.prompt: Combine the programme: a branded `RecordId`, a `Result`-returning parser, a generic iterable `Store<T>`, and an ambient host global. The input is `n` then `n` lines of `id value` (ids must match `r-\\d+`). Print `added <id>` or `rejected <line>` per line, then the stored ids space-separated in insertion order, then the store size.
exam.hint: Each piece is one week's idea: the brand proves validation happened, the Result forces the caller to branch, and Symbol.iterator makes the store spreadable.
