title: Java Mastery
subtitle: 26 weeks from `Scanner` to Dijkstra — the whole Java syllabus in order, with problems, a build project and an end-of-week exam.
intro: The interview-focused half of the app, sequenced. Each week gives you a few chapters, curated problems from the Library, something to build, and an exam — multiple choice plus a real coding final — that you must pass to unlock the next week. Weeks ahead stay sealed; weeks behind stay open.

weeks.title: Reading Input & Variables
weeks.goal: Get data in, get answers out, and name values with the right type.

problems.note: Whole-line input rather than a token.

weeks.project: Write a `Profile.java` that reads a name, an age and a city, then prints a three-line labelled summary — one variable per field, each explicitly typed.

quiz.question: Which Scanner call reads a whole line including spaces?
quiz.explanation: `next()` stops at whitespace and returns one token. Mixing `nextInt()` with `nextLine()` also famously leaves the newline behind — read it off deliberately.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `int` and `Integer`?
options: int is a primitive; Integer is an object wrapper that can be null
quiz.explanation: Collections can only hold objects, which is why `List<Integer>` exists — and why an unboxed null throws a NullPointerException.

quiz.question: What does `System.out.println(1 + 2 + "x")` print?
quiz.explanation: Evaluation is left to right: the two ints add first, then the result is concatenated. `"x" + 1 + 2` would give x12.

quiz.question: Which keyword allocates a new object and runs its constructor?
quiz.explanation: `new` reserves heap space and invokes the constructor, handing back a reference.

quiz.question: What does `void` as a return type mean?
quiz.explanation: `void` means the method produces no return value at all — you can't assign its result.

quiz.question: `continue` inside a loop will…
quiz.explanation: `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration; `break` is what exits the loop.

quiz.question: Which is TRUE about `var`?
options: The type is inferred from the initializer
It makes the variable dynamically typed
It means the value can't change
quiz.explanation: `var` is still statically typed — the compiler infers the type; it only works for local variables with an initializer.

quiz.question: `instanceof` evaluates to…
quiz.explanation: `o instanceof Dog` is a boolean test of whether `o`'s runtime type is Dog (or a subtype).

exam.title: Profile card
exam.prompt: The input is a name, an age and a city on one line. Print three labelled lines — `Name: ada`, `Age: 36`, `City: london` — then a fourth line with the age in dog years (age times 7).
exam.hint: Read the three tokens in order with next()/nextInt()/next(), then build each line with string concatenation.

weeks.title: Arithmetic & Booleans
weeks.goal: Integer division, remainder, and building conditions that read like the rule.

problems.note: A rule with nested exceptions — mind && over ||.

weeks.project: Write a `Change.java` that reads an amount in cents and prints how many quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies it takes, using only `/` and `%`.

quiz.question: What is `-7 / 2` in Java?
options: -3, because integer division truncates toward zero
quiz.explanation: Java truncates toward zero, so -7/2 is -3 and -7%2 is -1. Languages that floor instead (like Python) give -4 and 1.

quiz.question: Why does `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` fail for doubles?
options: Binary floating point cannot represent those decimals exactly
quiz.explanation: Compare with a tolerance, or use integers (cents) or BigDecimal when exactness matters.

quiz.question: What does short-circuit evaluation of `a && b` guarantee?
options: b is not evaluated when a is false
quiz.explanation: This is what makes `if (arr != null && arr.length > 0)` safe. The non-short-circuiting `&` would evaluate both and throw.

quiz.question: Which primitive is the DEFAULT type of an integer literal like `42`?
quiz.explanation: An un-suffixed integer literal is an `int`; append `L` for a `long`.

quiz.question: Converting `Integer` to `int` automatically is called…
quiz.explanation: Wrapper → primitive is unboxing; primitive → wrapper is autoboxing.

quiz.question: Which conversion REQUIRES an explicit cast?
quiz.explanation: Narrowing (bigger → smaller) can lose data, so Java forces an explicit cast.

quiz.question: `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` produces…
quiz.explanation: Integer arithmetic wraps around silently; exceeding MAX_VALUE flips to the most negative int.

quiz.question: For exact monetary math you should use…
quiz.explanation: `double`/`float` are binary approximations; `BigDecimal` stores exact decimal values.

exam.title: Coin breakdown
exam.prompt: The input is an amount in cents. Print how many quarters (25), dimes (10), nickels (5) and pennies (1) it takes, one per line, taking as many of each as possible in that order.
exam.hint: Divide to take the coins, then use % to keep only what is left before moving to the next denomination.

weeks.title: Conditionals & Loops
weeks.goal: Branch and repeat deliberately, with the right loop for the job.
weeks.project: Write a `Triangle.java` that reads `n` and prints a right triangle of `*`, then the same triangle right-aligned — one nested loop each.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `while` and `do-while`?
options: do-while always runs the body at least once
while can be broken out of; do-while cannot
quiz.explanation: `do-while` tests after the body, which is what you want for 'read, then decide whether to read again' loops.

quiz.question: What does `break` do inside nested loops?
options: Exits only the innermost loop, unless a label is used
quiz.explanation: `continue` skips one iteration; a labelled break (`outer: for ...` then `break outer;`) is how you leave several levels at once.

quiz.question: Why does `for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++)` over an array of length n break?
options: The last index is n - 1, so i == n is out of bounds
quiz.explanation: Off-by-one at the boundary is the most common array bug. The half-open convention `i < n` avoids it.

quiz.question: Which pair of properties do we use to judge an algorithm?
quiz.explanation: We ask two things of every algorithm: does it produce the right answer for all valid inputs (correctness), and how well does it scale (efficiency)?

quiz.question: You have two solutions: A is very fast but crashes on empty input; B is slower but always correct. Which is preferable as a starting point?
options: B, because correctness comes before efficiency
quiz.explanation: A wrong-but-fast answer is worthless. Correctness is the first requirement; you optimize only among solutions that are already correct.

quiz.question: Which of these disqualifies a procedure from being an algorithm?
options: It might never terminate on some inputs
It uses more than O(1) memory
quiz.explanation: An algorithm must be finite — it has to terminate. A procedure that can loop forever on some input is not an algorithm.

quiz.question: Why do we care about how cost grows with input size n rather than the raw time in seconds?
options: Raw time depends on the machine, language, and load; growth rate is intrinsic to the algorithm
quiz.explanation: Wall-clock time varies with hardware and language. The *growth rate* (Big-O) is a property of the algorithm itself, so it's what we reason about.

exam.title: Right triangle
exam.prompt: The input is one integer `n`. Print a left-aligned triangle of `*` with rows 1..n, then a blank line, then the same triangle right-aligned in a field of width `n` (padded with spaces).
exam.hint: Two nested loops per triangle: the inner one writes the padding, then the stars. Trailing spaces are trimmed by the judge, leading ones are not.

weeks.title: Overflow & Bit Manipulation
weeks.goal: Know when an int is not big enough, and work with the bits directly.
weeks.project: Write a `Bits.java` that reads an int and prints its 32-bit binary form, its popcount, and the value with only its lowest set bit kept (`n & -n`).

quiz.question: `int a = 2_000_000_000; int b = a + a;` — what is b?
options: A negative number; the addition wrapped around
quiz.explanation: Java's int arithmetic wraps silently. Widening one operand to long BEFORE the operation is the fix — casting the result afterwards is too late.

quiz.question: What does `n & (n - 1)` do?
quiz.explanation: Which is why `n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0` tests for a power of two, and why repeating it counts set bits.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `>>` and `>>>`?
options: >> keeps the sign bit; >>> shifts in zeros
quiz.explanation: For negative numbers `>>` preserves the sign while `>>>` does not — which is why `>>>` is used for the midpoint trick and hash mixing.

quiz.question: Which primitive is the DEFAULT type of an integer literal like `42`?
quiz.explanation: An un-suffixed integer literal is an `int`; append `L` for a `long`.

quiz.question: Converting `Integer` to `int` automatically is called…
quiz.explanation: Wrapper → primitive is unboxing; primitive → wrapper is autoboxing.

quiz.question: Which conversion REQUIRES an explicit cast?
quiz.explanation: Narrowing (bigger → smaller) can lose data, so Java forces an explicit cast.

quiz.question: `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` produces…
quiz.explanation: Integer arithmetic wraps around silently; exceeding MAX_VALUE flips to the most negative int.

quiz.question: For exact monetary math you should use…
quiz.explanation: `double`/`float` are binary approximations; `BigDecimal` stores exact decimal values.

quiz.question: Objects created with `new` live on the…
quiz.explanation: Objects go on the shared heap; local variables and call frames live on each thread's stack.

quiz.question: The difference between the JDK and the JRE is that the JDK also includes…
quiz.explanation: JRE = run Java; JDK = JRE + `javac` and tools to build it.

quiz.question: Deep infinite recursion typically causes…
quiz.explanation: Each call adds a stack frame; too many exhausts the thread's stack → StackOverflowError.

quiz.question: A memory leak in Java usually means…
options: you still hold references to objects you don't need
quiz.explanation: The GC only frees unreachable objects; lingering references (e.g. in a growing cache) keep them alive.

quiz.question: Bytecode (`.class`) is…
quiz.explanation: `javac` produces platform-independent bytecode; the JVM (optionally JIT-compiling) runs it.

quiz.question: Generational GC is based on the observation that…
quiz.explanation: The weak generational hypothesis: most objects become garbage quickly, so the young generation is collected often and cheaply.

exam.title: Bit report
exam.prompt: The input is one non-negative int. Print its 32-bit binary form with leading zeros, its popcount, the value with only the lowest set bit kept (`n & -n`), and whether it is a power of two.
exam.hint: Walk bits from 31 down to 0 for the binary string; `rest &= rest - 1` clears one set bit per pass, which counts them.

weeks.title: Digits, Number Theory & Modular Arithmetic
weeks.goal: Take numbers apart, factor them, and keep results inside a modulus.

problems.note: Compare without converting to a String.

weeks.project: Write a `Modpow.java` computing `base^exp mod m` by squaring, and check it against a slow loop for small inputs.

quiz.question: Why does trial division stop at `d * d <= n`?
options: Any factor above the square root pairs with one below it
quiz.explanation: Factors come in pairs around the square root, so finding none below it proves there are none at all.

quiz.question: Why compute LCM as `a / gcd * b` rather than `a * b / gcd`?
options: Dividing first keeps the intermediate value from overflowing
quiz.explanation: Both are mathematically equal, but `a * b` can overflow long before the division brings it back down.

quiz.question: Why take the modulus at every step of modular exponentiation?
options: It keeps every intermediate product inside the range of a long
It makes the result correct, which it otherwise would not be
It is only needed at the end
quiz.explanation: The maths works either way; the reduction is what stops the intermediate values overflowing.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of two nested loops that each run from 0 to n-1?
quiz.explanation: Nesting multiplies: n iterations × n iterations = n^2 → O(n^2).

quiz.question: The inner loop runs from i+1 to n-1 (shrinking as i grows). Overall complexity?
options: O(n) — because the inner loop shrinks
O(n^2) — the total is n(n-1)/2, still quadratic
quiz.explanation: Summing the shrinking bounds gives n(n-1)/2 ≈ n²/2. Dropping the constant, that's still O(n^2) — all-pairs work.

quiz.question: A loop that repeatedly halves n until it reaches 1 runs in:
quiz.explanation: Halving 16→8→4→2→1 takes log₂ n steps, so it's O(log n).

quiz.question: For the recurrence T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n), the total time is:
quiz.explanation: Two half-size subproblems plus linear work per level, over log n levels of n total work, gives O(n log n) — the merge-sort recurrence.

quiz.question: Appending to a dynamic array that doubles when full has which amortized cost per append?
quiz.explanation: Occasional O(n) doublings are rare enough that n appends cost ~2n total, i.e. O(1) amortized each.

quiz.question: Unless stated otherwise, 'the time complexity' of an algorithm refers to its:
quiz.explanation: By convention, an unqualified complexity is the worst case — the guarantee that holds for every input of size n.

weeks.title: Array Iteration & Patterns
weeks.goal: Scan an array once and answer several questions at the same time.

problems.note: Track two values in one pass.

weeks.project: Write a `Stats.java` that reads `n` then `n` numbers and prints min, max, sum, mean (2 decimals) and how many are above the mean — using no more than two passes.

quiz.question: Why seed a running maximum with `a[0]` rather than 0?
options: An all-negative array would otherwise report 0
quiz.explanation: Seeding with a real element (or Integer.MIN_VALUE) is what makes the scan correct for every input, not just non-negative ones.

quiz.question: What does `int[] b = a;` do?
options: Copies the reference — both names see the same array
Creates an empty array of the same length
quiz.explanation: Arrays are objects. `Arrays.copyOf` or `clone()` is what actually duplicates the contents.

quiz.question: What is `arr.length` versus `s.length()`?
options: Arrays expose a length FIELD; String exposes a length() METHOD
length() only works on char arrays
quiz.explanation: A small inconsistency in the language, and one of the most common compile errors when moving between the two.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search over n elements?
quiz.explanation: In the worst case the target is last or absent, so you examine all n elements → O(n).

quiz.question: Linear search requires the data to be sorted first.
quiz.explanation: False — linear search works on unsorted data with no preprocessing. That's one of its main advantages.

quiz.question: For finding the maximum of a list that may contain negative numbers, what should `best` start as?
options: The first element of the list
quiz.explanation: Starting at 0 breaks on all-negative lists (it would wrongly return 0). Initialize best to the first element.

quiz.question: You will search the SAME unsorted array thousands of times for different targets. Better than repeated linear search:
options: Build a hash set once (O(n)), then each lookup is O(1)
quiz.explanation: Repeated membership queries are the signal to preprocess into a hash set: O(n) once, then O(1) per lookup.

quiz.question: The 'running aggregate' scan (max/min/sum/count in one pass) has what space complexity?
quiz.explanation: It keeps only a constant number of accumulator variables, so O(1) auxiliary space.

exam.title: Array statistics

exam.hint: Seed min and max with a[0]. Cast to double BEFORE dividing, or integer division truncates the mean.

weeks.goal: Traverse text efficiently, and know when to drop to a char array.

problems.note: Two passes with a frequency table.

quiz.question: Why is building a string with `s += c` in a loop slow?
options: Strings are immutable, so each += allocates and copies a new string
quiz.explanation: That makes the loop O(n²). `StringBuilder` appends into a growable buffer and is the standard fix.

quiz.question: What does `s.charAt(i) - 'a'` give you?
options: The 0-based position of the letter in the alphabet
quiz.explanation: chars are integers, so subtracting 'a' maps 'a'..'z' onto 0..25 — the index into a 26-element counting array.

quiz.question: Why compare strings with `.equals()` rather than `==`?
options: == compares references, which differ for equal strings built at runtime
quiz.explanation: Literals are interned so `==` often appears to work, which makes the bug show up only once the string comes from input.

quiz.question: Java strings are immutable, so `s = s + "x"`…
quiz.explanation: Concatenation builds a brand-new String; the original is unchanged (which is why loops should use StringBuilder).

quiz.question: To compare the CONTENTS of two strings you should use…
quiz.explanation: `==` compares references; `.equals()` compares character content.

quiz.question: Building a string in a tight loop should use…
quiz.explanation: Repeated `+` creates many throwaway Strings; StringBuilder mutates one buffer.

quiz.question: The string pool means two identical string LITERALS…
quiz.explanation: Interned literals are cached, so `"a" == "a"` is often true — but never rely on `==` for content.

quiz.question: `StringBuffer` differs from `StringBuilder` in that it is…
quiz.explanation: StringBuffer's methods are synchronized; StringBuilder isn't, making it faster for single-threaded use.

It is always shorter than the input

options: Two offset arrays, dr = {1,-1,0,0} and dc = {0,0,1,-1}, in one loop
Four separate if blocks, which is the only correct way
A nested loop over the whole grid
quiz.explanation: The direction-array idiom keeps the bounds check in one place; the eight-neighbour version just extends the arrays.

quiz.question: Java strings are immutable, so `s = s + "x"`…
quiz.explanation: Concatenation builds a brand-new String; the original is unchanged (which is why loops should use StringBuilder).

quiz.question: To compare the CONTENTS of two strings you should use…

quiz.question: Building a string in a tight loop should use…

quiz.question: `StringBuffer` differs from `StringBuilder` in that it is…

quiz.question: A problem gives you a SORTED array and asks for a pair summing to a target. The signal points to:
quiz.explanation: 'Sorted' plus 'find a pair' is the classic two-pointers signal: move inward from both ends based on the current sum.

quiz.question: 'Longest contiguous subarray/substring satisfying a condition' most strongly signals:

quiz.question: You must return the k largest elements of a big stream. Best-matched tool?

A heap / priority queue of size k
quiz.explanation: A size-k heap keeps the top k without fully sorting everything — the standard 'top k' technique.

quiz.question: The problem asks for ALL permutations of a set. This signals:
quiz.explanation: 'All arrangements/combinations/subsets' means you must explore the full decision tree — that's backtracking.

weeks.title: Two Pointers & In-place Work
weeks.goal: Walk a sorted array from both ends, and rearrange without extra space.

problems.note: A write pointer trailing a read pointer.

weeks.project: Write a `Dutch.java` sorting an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass with three pointers — no sorting library call.

quiz.question: Why does the two-pointer sum walk require a SORTED array?
options: Sortedness is what makes 'too small' imply moving the low pointer
It does not; it works on any array
To allow binary search inside the loop
quiz.explanation: Without order, a smaller sum tells you nothing about which side to move, and the O(n) argument collapses.

quiz.question: What does the write-pointer idiom achieve in move-zeroes?
options: Compaction in place: the write index only advances on a kept element
quiz.explanation: Read every element, write only the ones you keep, then fill the tail — the standard in-place filter.

quiz.question: Rotating by reversal: reverse first k, reverse the rest, reverse the whole. Why does it work?
options: Each reversal puts a block in place while reversing it; the final one undoes that
It is a coincidence of index arithmetic
It only works when k divides n
quiz.explanation: Three linear reversals give an O(n) time, O(1) space rotation — much simpler than juggling with cycle following.

quiz.question: The converging two-pointer technique (one at each end) assumes the array is:
options: A power of two in length
quiz.explanation: Converging pointers rely on order: a too-small sum means move left inward, too-big means move right inward. That logic needs a sorted array.

quiz.question: In a sorted-array pair-sum search, the current sum is LESS than the target. You should:
quiz.explanation: To increase the sum, advance the left pointer to a larger value. Moving right inward would shrink the sum further.

quiz.question: Why is two pointers O(n) even though there are two indices?
options: Because each pointer only moves forward/inward, advancing at most n times total
quiz.explanation: Neither pointer ever backtracks, so across the whole run each advances ≤ n times — linear total work.

quiz.question: Which problem fits the SLOW/FAST (same-direction) variant rather than converging ends?
options: Check if a string is a palindrome
Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place
Find a pair summing to a target in a sorted array
quiz.explanation: In-place dedup uses a slow pointer marking the deduped prefix and a fast pointer scanning ahead — a same-direction pattern.

quiz.question: Detecting a cycle in a linked list with Floyd's algorithm uses:
options: A slow pointer and a fast pointer moving twice as fast
quiz.explanation: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare moves one pointer 1 step and the other 2 steps; if there's a cycle they eventually meet.

weeks.title: Sliding Window
weeks.goal: Maintain a window instead of recomputing every subarray.

problems.note: A running minimum, which is the degenerate case.

weeks.project: Write a `Window.java` that reads `n k` and `n` numbers and prints the maximum, minimum and average of every window of size k — one pass.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a fixed and a variable window?
options: A fixed window always moves both ends together; a variable one grows until a condition breaks, then shrinks
A variable window can move backwards
quiz.explanation: The variable form is the one that solves 'longest substring with property P' — grow greedily, shrink only while the property is violated.

quiz.question: Why is the sliding-window sum O(n) rather than O(n·k)?
options: Each step adds the entering element and subtracts the leaving one
quiz.explanation: Reusing the previous window's answer is the whole trick — the same idea as a prefix sum, computed incrementally.

quiz.question: A window over an array with negative numbers — which pattern breaks?
options: Variable-size windows that assume growing the window grows the sum
quiz.explanation: Monotonicity is the hidden precondition of the shrink step. With negatives you usually need prefix sums plus a map instead.

quiz.question: Sliding window is the right tool when the problem concerns a … subarray or substring.
quiz.explanation: Windows model contiguous runs. If the elements needn't be adjacent, a window doesn't apply.

quiz.question: When a fixed-size window of width k slides one step to the right, you should:
options: Recompute the sum of all k elements
Add the new right element and subtract the element that just left
quiz.explanation: Incremental update is the whole point: +new right, −old left keeps each step O(1) instead of O(k).

quiz.question: In a variable-size window, when the window becomes INVALID you should:
options: Shrink from the left until it's valid again
quiz.explanation: Contract from the left to restore validity, then continue expanding right — that's the expand/contract pattern.

quiz.question: Why is the variable-size window O(n) despite the inner while-loop that shrinks left?
options: Because each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so total moves are ≤ 2n
Because the window is fixed size
quiz.explanation: left and right each advance at most n times over the whole run, so the combined work is linear even with the inner loop.

quiz.question: Recomputing each window from scratch instead of updating incrementally makes a size-k window cost:
quiz.explanation: Recomputing k elements for each of ~n positions is O(n·k) — the incremental update is what brings it down to O(n).

exam.title: Window report
exam.prompt: The input is `n k` then `n` integers. For every window of `k` consecutive values print `max min sum` on its own line, then the largest window sum on the final line.
exam.hint: Seed best with Long.MIN_VALUE so an all-negative array reports the real maximum rather than 0.

quiz.explanation: The off-by-one is exactly why the prefix array is given an extra leading zero — it makes l = 0 work without a special case.

options: A subarray sums to k exactly when two prefix sums differ by k
quiz.explanation: Counting earlier prefixes equal to `current - k` turns an O(n²) scan into one pass.

quiz.question: What does a difference array give you?
options: O(1) range UPDATES, with one final pass to materialise the values
quiz.explanation: It is the dual of a prefix sum: prefix sums make queries cheap, difference arrays make updates cheap.

quiz.question: With prefix[0]=0 and prefix[k]=a[0]+…+a[k-1], the sum of a[i..j] inclusive equals:
quiz.explanation: With the 0-sentinel and size-(n+1) prefix, rangeSum(i,j) = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i].

quiz.question: After an O(n) build, each range-sum query costs:
quiz.explanation: A range sum is a single subtraction of two prefix entries → O(1) per query.

options: ask for exactly one range sum
ask for many range sums over the same array
quiz.explanation: The O(n) setup pays off across repeated queries. For a single query, a plain O(n) scan is simpler and equally fast.

quiz.question: What does the prefix[0] = 0 sentinel buy you?
options: It removes the special case when the range starts at index 0
quiz.explanation: The 0-sentinel makes prefix[j+1] - prefix[i] correct even when i = 0, avoiding a separate branch.

quiz.question: To apply many 'add v to every element in [i, j]' updates efficiently, use:
options: A difference array: diff[i] += v, diff[j+1] -= v, then prefix-sum once
quiz.explanation: A difference array records each range-add in O(1) at the two endpoints, then one prefix-sum pass reconstructs the final array.

quiz.question: Why mark a cell visited as you ENQUEUE it rather than when you dequeue it?
options: Otherwise the same cell can be enqueued several times before processing
quiz.explanation: Marking on dequeue lets duplicates pile up in the queue, which can blow up the memory and the running time.

quiz.question: Why is a recursive flood fill risky on a large grid?
options: The recursion depth can equal the number of cells and overflow the stack
quiz.explanation: An explicit stack or a BFS queue has the same complexity without depending on the JVM's stack size.

quiz.question: What is a common trick to avoid a separate visited array?
options: Overwrite each visited cell with a sentinel value in the grid itself
Use a HashSet of coordinates, which is always faster
quiz.explanation: It saves memory and is fine when the grid may be mutated — otherwise copy first or use a boolean array.

quiz.question: You store every element you've seen in a hash set while scanning an array of size n. Auxiliary space is:
quiz.explanation: The set can hold up to n distinct elements, so it uses O(n) extra memory.

quiz.question: A recursive function that recurses to a depth of n uses how much space just for the call stack?
quiz.explanation: Each pending call keeps a stack frame alive, so depth-n recursion costs O(n) stack space even with tiny frames.

quiz.question: The 'seen set' trick turns an O(n^2)-time duplicate check into O(n) time. What is it spending to do that?

Spending O(n) memory to make queries faster
Reducing both time and space to zero
quiz.explanation: You build an O(n) array once so that later queries drop from O(n) to O(1) — spending memory to buy query speed.

weeks.title: Recursion, Backtracking & Pruning
weeks.goal: Explore a decision tree, undo cleanly, and cut branches that cannot win.
weeks.project: Write a `Sudoku.java` that reads a 9x9 grid and reports whether it is solvable, using constraint checks to prune before recursing.

quiz.question: What distinguishes backtracking from plain recursion?
options: It UNDOES its choice after recursing, so siblings see a clean state
quiz.explanation: The undo step is the definition. Forgetting it is why the second branch of a search returns nonsense.

quiz.question: Why does naive recursive Fibonacci take exponential time?
options: The same subproblems are recomputed along different branches
quiz.explanation: Memoising collapses it to linear. Recognising overlapping subproblems is the step from recursion to dynamic programming.

quiz.question: What is the point of a pruning check?
options: Abandon a branch as soon as it cannot possibly lead to a solution
quiz.explanation: It does not change the worst case, but on real inputs it is often the difference between milliseconds and never finishing.

quiz.question: What two ingredients does every correct recursive function need?
options: A base case and a recursive case that shrinks toward it
A hash map and a set
quiz.explanation: A base case tells it when to stop; the recursive case must make progress toward that base case, or it never terminates.

quiz.question: Recursion of depth d uses how much memory just for the call stack?
quiz.explanation: Each pending call keeps a live stack frame, so depth-d recursion costs O(d) stack space.

quiz.question: A recursive function with no reachable base case will most likely:
quiz.explanation: Without a base case (or without progressing toward it), it recurses forever, exhausting the stack — a stack overflow.

quiz.question: The recursive factorial uses O(n) space while the loop version uses O(1). The extra space in the recursive one is:
options: The call stack of n frames
quiz.explanation: The recursion stacks n frames before any returns, costing O(n); the loop keeps a single accumulator, O(1).

quiz.question: Which problem shape is MOST naturally expressed with recursion?
quiz.explanation: Trees are defined recursively (a node plus subtrees), so recursive traversal mirrors the structure directly.

quiz.question: The 'leap of faith' when writing recursion means:
options: Assume the recursive call already correctly solves the smaller subproblem, and just combine it
quiz.explanation: You trust that the recursion handles the smaller input correctly and focus on the combine step — correctness then follows by induction.

quiz.question: In the recurrence T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n), what does f(n) represent?
options: The work to divide and combine outside the recursive calls
quiz.explanation: f(n) is the non-recursive work per call — splitting the input and combining subresults. a and n/b describe the recursive calls.

quiz.question: Merge sort is T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n). By the Master Theorem this is:
quiz.explanation: log₂2 = 1 so n^c = n, and f(n) = n matches it → Case 2 → O(n log n).

quiz.question: Binary search is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1). This solves to:
quiz.explanation: a=1, b=2 gives n^0 = 1, and f(n)=O(1) matches → Case 2 → O(1·log n) = O(log n).

quiz.question: The Master Theorem in the a·T(n/b)+f(n) form does NOT directly apply to which recurrence?
quiz.explanation: T(n-1) is a subtract-and-conquer form, not a divide form (n/b). The Master Theorem is for divide recurrences; this one just unrolls to O(n).

quiz.question: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + O(1) unrolls to which complexity?
quiz.explanation: Doubling the number of calls at each of n levels gives 2^n total — the classic exponential blowup of naive branching recursion.

quiz.question: In the Master Theorem, which case ADDS a logarithmic factor to the result?
quiz.explanation: Case 2 is the balanced case where per-level work is equal across log n levels, contributing the extra log factor (e.g. n log n).

options: A greedy choice and a tie-break
quiz.explanation: Without overlap, memoising buys nothing; without optimal substructure, combining subproblem answers is simply invalid.

quiz.question: Simplify: 4n^2 + 100n + 3000 in Big-O.
quiz.explanation: Keep only the dominant term (n^2) and drop constant factors and lower-order terms → O(n^2).

quiz.question: An algorithm makes two separate full passes over an array of size n, one after the other. Its complexity is:
quiz.explanation: Sequential phases add: n + n = 2n, and constant factors drop, so it's O(n). Nesting (not sequencing) would give O(n^2).

quiz.question: Which growth rate is best (scales best) for large n?
quiz.explanation: Order is O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2). Logarithmic grows slowest, so it scales best.

quiz.question: You combine an O(n) step followed by an O(n log n) sort. Total complexity?
quiz.explanation: Sequential steps add, and the sum is dominated by the larger term: O(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n).

quiz.explanation: For O(n^2), replacing n with 2n gives (2n)^2 = 4n^2 — four times the work. That ×4 fingerprint means quadratic.

quiz.question: The problem says n can be up to 200,000 and the time limit is tight. Which target complexity is the safe aim?
quiz.explanation: At n = 2×10^5, O(n^2) is ~4×10^10 operations — far too slow. O(n log n) (~3.5 million) comfortably fits, so aim there or better.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of two nested loops that each run from 0 to n-1?
quiz.explanation: Nesting multiplies: n iterations × n iterations = n^2 → O(n^2).

quiz.question: The inner loop runs from i+1 to n-1 (shrinking as i grows). Overall complexity?
options: O(n) — because the inner loop shrinks
O(n^2) — the total is n(n-1)/2, still quadratic
quiz.explanation: Summing the shrinking bounds gives n(n-1)/2 ≈ n²/2. Dropping the constant, that's still O(n^2) — all-pairs work.

quiz.question: A loop that repeatedly halves n until it reaches 1 runs in:
quiz.explanation: Halving 16→8→4→2→1 takes log₂ n steps, so it's O(log n).

quiz.question: For the recurrence T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n), the total time is:
quiz.explanation: Two half-size subproblems plus linear work per level, over log n levels of n total work, gives O(n log n) — the merge-sort recurrence.

quiz.question: Appending to a dynamic array that doubles when full has which amortized cost per append?
quiz.explanation: Occasional O(n) doublings are rare enough that n appends cost ~2n total, i.e. O(1) amortized each.

quiz.question: Unless stated otherwise, 'the time complexity' of an algorithm refers to its:
quiz.explanation: By convention, an unqualified complexity is the worst case — the guarantee that holds for every input of size n.

The priority queue cannot hold negatives

the map ran out of capacity
